results.title: Call Center Complaint Handling: A 6-Step Guide
results.content:
### Product or Service Problems

This is one of the most straightforward types of complaints: the product is broken, or the service didn't work as advertised. Customers are often frustrated because their expectations haven't been met. They might have received a faulty item, encountered a bug in your software, or found that a service didn't deliver the promised results. For your agents, resolving these issues requires a deep understanding of your offerings and clear procedures for troubleshooting, returns, or exchanges. Having a reliable knowledge base they can trust is non-negotiable. It allows them to find accurate information quickly and guide the customer to the right solution on the first try.

### Billing and Payment Errors [...] For a contact center, this process is your bread and butter. Your agents are on the front lines, turning frustrating moments into opportunities for connection. A solid complaint handling strategy isn't just about damage control; it's a powerful tool for gathering honest feedback and making your business better. When you see complaints as valuable data points, you can start to identify trends, fix broken processes, and refine your products or services. This proactive approach moves your team from simply reacting to problems to actively shaping a better customer experience.

### The High Stakes of Getting It Wrong [...] ### Document for Quality and Training

Every complaint should be documented in a centralized system. This isn't just about record-keeping; it's about building a library of real-world scenarios for quality and training. When you log the customer's issue, the steps the agent took, and the final resolution, you create a detailed case study. Your quality assurance team can use these records to review performance and ensure consistency. These documented complaints become powerful assets for your training programs, providing concrete examples that help new and existing agents learn how to handle difficult situations effectively. A connected quality assurance platform makes it easy to link these interaction records directly to agent scorecards and coaching sessions.

### Use Data to Spot Trends

results.title: How to Handle Customer Complaints (Step by Step)
results.content:
Process: Workflow or policy gaps, such as a customer who received no shipping confirmation or was transferred between three departments.
 Product: Defects or missing features, such as a broken integration or a report that won’t export.
 People: Agent errors or training gaps, such as incorrect information given on a previous call.
 Policy: Terms the customer finds unfair, such as a refund window they consider too short or an SLA exclusion they weren’t aware of.

Pairing each category with the same seven log fields keeps the data consistent across agents and channels. [...] | Log field | What to record |
 --- |
| Date | When the complaint was received |
| Channel | Which channel the customer used |
| Root-cause category | Process, Product, People or Policy |
| Sub-category | The specifics, such as “no shipping confirmation” |
| Resolution applied | What the agent did to fix it |
| Time to resolve | Hours or days from first contact to confirmation |
| Customer sentiment at close | A rating on a three-point scale |

Root-cause logging is a training tool as well as a reporting function. Complaints that cluster under People point to a coaching gap, and complaints that cluster under Process point to an ops fix.

## How the steps change on phone, email and chat [...] Logging the root cause turns each resolved complaint into data that can prevent future complaints, but only if the team captures it the same way every time. Tagging complaints by category turns individual tickets into a pattern map for product and ops teams. Reviewing the log monthly shows which categories are growing and where an upstream fix would cut complaint volume.

A four-category taxonomy keeps tagging fast enough for agents to do in real time.

#### 1. The Order Didn’t Arrive on Time

Customers put their faith in promised delivery dates, and assume brands are savvy enough to 1) accurately predict tracking, and 2) update customers about anticipated delays. If an order isn’t fulfilled in a timely way, it can spark a very angry response.

The agent’s first order of business: track the customer’s package. If it’s marked as delivered, ask the customer to confirm the address. Maybe the package was left in a different location than they’re used to, or was marked delivered but left on the truck – it happens. If the package is still in transit, try something like this.

Dear [First name],

I’m so sorry your order hasn’t arrived. I know how frustrating this must be. [...] When responding to angry emails, your agents will need to walk a very fine line: They’ll need to respond quickly, but in a way that projects warmth, concern, and a take-charge attitude. They’ll need to be succinct, while conveying their commitment to righting the wrong and explaining how the problem will be solved.

results.title: The Most Common Complaints Filed Against Real Estate Agents
results.content:
Revised on October 16th, 2026

As a real estate agent, your reputation rests on professionalism, honesty, and trustworthiness. Most agents go their entire careers without a formal complaint, but when complaints do happen, they tend to follow familiar patterns. Knowing those patterns is one of the best ways to avoid them. In this blog, we analyze some of the most common complaints filed against real estate agents.

### Misrepresentation of Property [...] ### What Happens After a Complaint

A complaint doesn’t automatically mean a violation. Commissions investigate, and many complaints are dismissed. When a violation is confirmed, consequences can include fines, required education, probation, suspension, or revocation of the license. Clients who believe they were harmed can also pursue civil claims, and a complaint can affect your reputation and your ability to earn referrals long after the case closes.

The most useful thing an agent can do is treat every transaction as if it may someday be reviewed. Clear records, honest conversations, and prompt communication go a long way toward keeping a small misunderstanding from becoming a formal complaint.

### The Importance of Professionalism, Honesty, and Trust [...] ### Failing to Present Offers

Agents are expected to present all written offers to their clients, regardless of whether the agent thinks the offer is strong enough. Deciding on the client’s behalf that an offer isn’t worth presenting, or screening out an offer because the agent expects the seller will reject it, can be treated as a breach of the agent’s duty. The decision belongs to the client.

How to protect yourself: Present every offer promptly, even when you advise against it. Your job is to give your honest opinion and then let the client decide.
